exam_tips: Suspected phish: report it (Report Phishing button / SOC), do not click, reply or forward it to colleagues.
Lookalike domain (examp1e.com) = typosquatting; wire-transfer request from a 'CEO' = BEC / impersonation.
'Employee plugs in a USB drive found in the car park' = removable media training (baiting).
Risky = intentional, unexpected = deviates from baseline, unintentional = accident: know the three words.
Initial vs recurring is about training cadence; computer-based training (CBT) and gamification are delivery methods.

| with access reviews/recertification.

|   • 'Access based on attributes like location or time' => ABAC.
|   • Mandatory vacation and job rotation are detective controls that also
| expose SoD fraud.

| Objective: SY0-701 1.2 Zero Trust (control plane vs data plane) and 4.6
| conditional access.

| Key Concepts
|   • Control plane = Policy Engine (decides) + Policy Administrator
| (issues/revokes). Data plane = PEP + resources.
|   • Adaptive identity: the same user gets ALLOW, STEP_UP or DENY depending
| on real-time context.
|   • Threat scope reduction: tokens are short-lived and scoped to ONE
| resource + action.
|   • Never trust, always verify: the PEP re-validates on every request,
| even inside the network.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Treating 'on the VPN' or 'inside the LAN' as trusted (implicit trust
| zone).

| movement.

| it.

| entitlements and device/workload posture.

| never standing credentials.
|   • The PE should weigh agent-specific risk signals (anomalous call
| volume, new tool usage).
|   • The PA must be able to revoke an agent's tokens instantly (kill
| switch).

|   • 'Establishes and terminates the session / issues tokens' => Policy
| Administrator.
|   • Zero Trust replaces perimeter trust with continuous, per-request
| verification.
|   • Microsegmentation and implicit trust zones are data-plane concepts.

|   • Containment actions (blocking an IP, disabling an account) should
| require human approval on high-impact assets.
|

|   • 'Many failed logins for many accounts from one source' => password
| spraying.
|   • 'User logged in from two countries 30 minutes apart' => impossible
| travel.
|   • 'Prove evidence was not altered' => hashing / chain of custody.
|   • Missing or out-of-cycle logs are themselves an indicator of
| compromise.

questions.prompt: An attacker deletes one line from a sealed log set. What does hash-chain verification report?
questions.explanation: The recomputed chain diverges from the sealed manifest at the deleted position. MANIFEST_FORGED is only reported when the manifest's own HMAC fails.

questions.prompt: Why is the log manifest HMAC-signed instead of only SHA-256 hashed?
choices: A plain hash can be recomputed by the attacker; an HMAC needs the secret key
questions.answer: A plain hash can be recomputed by the attacker; an HMAC needs the secret key
questions.explanation: Hashing gives integrity. Keyed hashing (HMAC) adds authenticity, because only the key holder could have produced the tag.

|   • 'Who approves changes' => Change Advisory Board (CAB); emergency
| changes go through an ECAB.
|   • 'Scheduled time to make changes with minimal business impact' =>
| maintenance window.

| technical implications in 1.3.

| Objective: SY0-701 4.7 (automation & orchestration guardrails) + 4.6 PAM

| Key Concepts
|   • Every agent is a non-human identity with its own least-privilege
| allow-list — never a shared admin account.
|   • Three-tier verdicts: ALLOW (in policy), REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL
| (uncertain/high impact), BLOCK (hard boundary).
|   • Hard boundaries are non-overridable: even a human can't approve
| disabling MFA through the agent pipeline.
|   • A kill switch (quarantine) stops runaway or hijacked automation after
| repeated violations.

| (no blast-radius limit).
|   • Trusting the agent's own references: it can invent ticket numbers,
| patch IDs and hostnames.
|   • Indirect prompt injection — data the agent reads (tickets, emails,
| logs) tells it to break policy.
|   • No rate limit: a looping agent restarts production 400 times before
| anyone notices.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Validate every agent claim against an authoritative source (CMDB,
| patch catalog, ticketing system).
|   • Route privileged or irreversible actions through the same CAB/approval
| workflow as humans.
|   • Keep a tamper-evident ledger of every proposed AND executed action for
| accountability.
|   • Separate duties: the agent that proposes a change must not be the
| identity that approves it.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Automation benefits: enforcing baselines, standard configurations,
| scaling securely, reaction time.
|   • Automation risks listed in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of
| failure, technical debt, ongoing supportability.
|   • 'Guard rails' in 4.7 = automated limits that keep scripts/agents
| inside safe boundaries.
|   • Human-in-the-loop is the governance answer whenever impact is high and
| confidence is low.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative
| analysis, strategies, BIA).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE
| reduction > its annual cost.
|   • Strategies: mitigate, transfer (insurance), avoid (stop the activity),
| accept, or exception/exemption.
|   • RPO = how much data you can lose (drives backup frequency); RTO = how
| long you can be down (drives restore design).
|   • MTBF measures reliability, MTTR measures repairability; availability =
| MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Buying a $500k control to protect against a $30k/yr ALE (security
| theatre).
|   • Treating low-likelihood/high-impact events as 'won't happen' instead
| of transferring them.
|   • Backups run nightly while the business assumed an RPO of 4 hours,
| discovered only after an outage.
|   • Risks accepted informally with no owner, no expiry date and no
| register entry.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI risk-analyst agent can compute ALE and draft treatments, but a
| named human risk OWNER must accept.
|   • Agents must cite the inputs (AV, EF, ARO sources) so assessments can
| be audited and challenged.
|   • AI agents themselves belong in the risk register: model failure,
| prompt injection and over-permissioning are risks too.
|   • Any agent with production write access raises the impact (SLE) of a
| compromise. Price that in.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Expect arithmetic: AV $100k, EF 25%, ARO 2 → SLE $25k, ALE $50k.
|   • 'Purchasing cyber insurance' = transfer. 'Discontinuing the service' =
| avoid.
|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative

| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE

| be audited and challenged.

| Objective: SY0-701 5.2 Risk management (quantitative & qualitative

| Key Concepts
|   • SLE = AV × EF; ALE = SLE × ARO. A control is worth buying when ALE

|   • 'Maximum tolerable data loss' = RPO. 'Maximum tolerable downtime to
| restore' = RTO.
|   • Risk appetite = how much risk the org will pursue; risk tolerance =
| acceptable deviation; threshold = trigger level.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Incident IR-2026-0042 -------------------------------------------------
| EDR flags malware (invoice_Q4.pdf.exe) on WS-0142 beaconing to
| 45.155.205.233. The same IP brute-forced and logged in as jdoe, who then
| cleared the DC01 Security log.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Playbook: rookie  →  score 0/100  (grade F) -----------------------------

Timeline
#  Phase        Action
-  -----------  ------
1  detection    Triage the EDR alert and correlate it with SIEM data
2  containment  Pull the power plug on WS-0142
3  analysis     Copy suspicious files to a personal USB stick to look at later
4  eradication  Reimage WS-0142 from the golden image
5  recovery     Return WS-0142 to service; restore user data from known-good backup
6  analysis     Capture a RAM image of WS-0142 and hash it (SHA-256)
7  containment  Disable jdoe and revoke all sessions/tokens

Issues
Step  Code                Penalty  Detail
----  ------------------  -------  ------
2     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'power_off': Destroys volatile evidence (RAM, network state, temp files)
2     EVIDENCE_DESTROYED  -20      'power_off' destroys uncollected evidence: ['CPU registers / cache', 'RAM, process table, network state', 'swap / temp files']
3     ANTI_PATTERN        -10      'copy_usb_unhashed': No hash, no write blocker, personal media: chain of custody is broken

| Objective: SY0-701 4.8 Incident response process & digital forensics.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Lifecycle: preparation → detection → analysis → containment →
| eradication → recovery → lessons learned.
|   • Order of volatility (RFC 3227): registers/cache → RAM & network state
| → swap/temp → disk → remote logs → archives.
|   • Chain of custody: who collected what, when, with which hash, and every
| hand-off since. One gap and the evidence can be thrown out.
|   • A legal hold freezes deletion of relevant data the moment litigation
| is reasonably anticipated.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Pulling the plug 'to stop the malware': RAM-resident malware and
| network state are gone forever.
|   • Reimaging before imaging the disk: no root cause analysis, no evidence
| for law enforcement or insurers.
|   • Restoring service before eradication: re-infection from the
| persistence you never found.
|   • Skipping lessons learned, so the playbook never improves.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI responders should follow the SAME lifecycle; enforce phase gates
| (no eradication until containment is confirmed).
|   • Agents may collect evidence but must hash it at acquisition and write
| to an append-only custody ledger.
|   • Destructive actions (power off, reimage, delete) need human sign-off
| and must check that evidence was acquired first.
|   • Log every agent action into the incident timeline; the agent's own
| actions are evidence too.
|

|   • 'What should be collected first?' → the most volatile source available
| (usually RAM).
|   • 'Stop the spread' = containment; 'remove the malware' = eradication;
| 'return to normal' = recovery.
|   • 'Documents everyone who handled the evidence' = chain of custody.
|   • Tabletop exercise = discussion-based; simulation = hands-on practice
| of the plan.

| Objective: SY0-701 4.7 Automation & orchestration (SOAR) tying together
| 1.2, 1.3, 4.6, 4.8 and 4.9.

| Key Concepts
|   • Detection, decision and execution are separate trust boundaries; no
| single component (or agent) owns all three.
|   • Every automated action is routed to the control that owns it: IAM for
| accounts, CAB for network changes, IR for hosts.
|   • Emergency changes still get an RFC, ECAB approval, a rehearsed backout
| and a post-implementation review.
|   • Human-in-the-loop on user-impacting actions turns false positives into
| rule-tuning instead of outages.

|   • A SOAR playbook that disables accounts automatically locks out the CEO
| on a false positive.

| default firewall rule.

|   • Give the SOC agent a narrow allow-list and let it PROPOSE; the
| Governor and humans DISPOSE.

| for approved agent actions: defense in depth.

| that triggered impossible travel.

| overturn it, and blocked attempts.

| act on SIEM alerts.
|   • Benefits in 4.7: efficiency, enforcing baselines, reaction time,
| workforce multiplier.
|   • Considerations in 4.7: complexity, cost, single point of failure,
| technical debt, ongoing supportability.
|   • Containment choices (isolate, segment, disable) must balance evidence
| preservation against spread.

|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).

| it assigns.

|   • CVSS bands: 9.0–10 Critical, 7.0–8.9 High, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 0.1–3.9
| Low.
|   • 'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating
| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.

| Key Concepts
|   • CVSS is a severity score, not a risk score. Risk adds asset
| criticality, exposure and active exploitation (KEV).

| insurance, or a time-boxed exception.

| 'done' is not proof.
|   • Assets missing from the inventory are the most dangerous: nobody
| patches what nobody owns.

|   • Sorting by CVSS alone, so a 9.8 on a lab box outranks a KEV 7.5 on an
| internet-facing gateway.
|   • Exceptions with no expiry, approved by whoever asked, renewed forever.
|   • Waiting for a patch on a zero-day instead of applying compensating
| controls today.
|   • Closing findings without rescanning: the patch failed silently.

|   • An AI triage agent may score and rank findings, but exceptions need an
| authorised human risk owner.
|   • Agents must take criticality and exposure from the CMDB, never infer
| or invent them; unknown assets mean worst case.
|   • Auto-patching agents go through change control (Lab 4) and must
| trigger a validation rescan afterwards.
|   • Log the agent's scoring inputs so a human can reproduce any priority
| it assigns.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • CVSS bands: 9.0–10 Critical, 7.0–8.9 High, 4.0–6.9 Medium, 0.1–3.9
| Low.
|   • 'Cannot patch, so add a control that reduces the risk' = compensating
| control.
|   • 'Formally accept a vulnerability for a defined time' =
| exception/exemption.
|   • TOC/TOU = race condition; malicious update = supply chain; no vendor
| fix yet = zero-day.

| exception/exemption.

| Objective: SY0-701 4.5 Email security (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, gateways) and 2.2
| message-based threat vectors.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • SPF authorises sending IPs for the ENVELOPE domain; DKIM signs the
| message for the d= domain.
|   • DMARC ties them to the visible From: SPF or DKIM must pass AND align
| with the From domain; p= says what to do on failure.
|   • Authentication proves where mail came from, not that it is safe: a
| lookalike domain can pass SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
|   • Content signals (impersonation, urgency, mismatched links, double
| extensions) catch what authentication cannot.
|

|   • Publishing DMARC p=none forever: you can see the spoofing but never
| block it.
|   • Trusting an Authentication-Results header added by an untrusted hop.

| 'external sender' banner.
|   • Blocking .exe but not .pdf.exe, .iso, .lnk or macro-enabled documents.
|

|   • An AI mail-triage agent may quarantine and add banners; releasing
| quarantined mail or allow-listing senders needs a human.
|   • Mail content is untrusted input: an email that tells the agent to
| 'mark this sender safe' is prompt injection.
|   • Agents must base verdicts on recomputed SPF/DKIM/DMARC, never on
| headers the sender controls.
|   • Log every agent verdict with its indicators so false positives can be
| tuned, as in the Lab 8 feedback loop.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • SPF = which servers may send · DKIM = digital signature on the message
| · DMARC = policy + alignment + reporting.
|   • BEC/impersonation: 'CEO' from a free-mail address asking for a wire
| transfer or changed bank details.
|   • Typosquatting / brand impersonation: micros0ft-support.com,
| paypa1.com.
|   • Secure email gateways enforce these checks at the perimeter; S/MIME
| provides end-to-end signing/encryption.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.

| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.

| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.

|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.

| control with rollback (Lab 4).

| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.

| attach the remediation step.

| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 4.1 Secure baselines: establish, deploy, maintain;
| hardening targets and techniques.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • A secure baseline is the approved minimum configuration; deploy it
| with GPO/MDM/config management, then measure drift.
|   • Hardening = reduce attack surface: remove unneeded services, enforce
| password/lockout policy, enable host firewall, EDR and auditing.
|   • Unknown is non-compliant: a setting the scanner can't read is treated
| as failed until proven otherwise.
|   • Exceptions are documented, ticketed, compensated and time-boxed, never
| silent.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

|   • Hardening once at build time and never re-scanning, so configuration
| drift goes unnoticed.
|   • Someone re-enables Print Spooler on a domain controller 'to print one
| report' (PrintNightmare).
|   • Turning off the host firewall or EDR to troubleshoot and never turning
| it back on.
|   • Baselines kept in a PDF instead of enforced as code.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • A remediation agent may apply baseline settings, but only via change
| control with rollback (Lab 4).
|   • Agents must never weaken a baseline (disable firewall/EDR/auditing);
| that is a Lab 5 protected-control BLOCK.
|   • Drift alerts are a great agent job: detect, explain, open a ticket,
| attach the remediation step.
|   • Approving a deviation (exception) stays a human decision with an
| expiry date.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Establish → deploy → maintain' is the secure-baseline lifecycle.
|   • Disabling unnecessary ports/services and default accounts is classic
| hardening.
|   • Configuration drift = systems slowly diverging from the baseline;
| detect with periodic scans.
|   • Group Policy (Windows) and SELinux (Linux mandatory access control)
| both appear in 4.1.

Recovery capability
System        Target RTO/RPO  Host fail RTO/RPO  Site loss RTO/RPO                        Restore  Verdict
------------  --------------  -----------------  ---------------------------------------  -------  -------
payroll-app   8h / 4h         8.5h / 24h         172.5h / 24h                             4.5h     GAPS
web-frontend  1h / 24h        0h / 15m           1h / 15m                                 18m      MEETS_TARGETS
auth-service  1h / 15m        15m / 15m          1h / 15m                                 22.8m    GAPS
erp-legacy    4h / 1h         15.25h / 24h       ∞ (cannot recover) / ∞ (cannot recover)  11.25h   GAPS
file-server   24h / 24h       5.5h / 24h         not required                             1.5h     MEETS_TARGETS

--- Step 2 — Gaps and cheapest fixes ----------------------------------------
payroll-app — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 8.5h (rebuild + differential restore) > target 8h
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 4h
  • SITE: cold site recovery takes 172.5h > target 8h
  • SITE RPO: after a site loss up to 24h of data is lost > target 4h
  • TEST: DR failover last tested 2025-01-10 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Back up at least every 4h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Use a hot site (ready in 1h, $500,000/yr)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
web-frontend — MEETS_TARGETS
  • All targets met and tested.
auth-service — GAPS
  • DISK: RAID0 tolerates 0 disk failure(s) < required 1
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 10.2m < required 4h
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID5 (tolerates 1, 75% usable capacity)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
erp-legacy — GAPS
  • RTO: host failure takes 15.25h (rebuild + incremental restore) > target 4h
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 1h
  • SITE: no offsite copy of the data (no replication, backups kept onsite)
  • SITE: no recovery site, so nowhere to restore to after a site loss
  • TEST: backup restore never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • TEST: DR failover never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add active-passive clustering (failover 15m, $30,000/yr)
  • → Back up at least every 1h (snapshots/journaling between full backups)
  • → Keep an offsite/cloud backup copy (3-2-1) or replicate to the recovery site
  • → Contract a hot site
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
file-server — MEETS_TARGETS
  • All targets met and tested.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.

| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.

|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 1 — Achieved vs target (as of 2026-11-03) --------------------------

Recovery capability
System        Target RTO/RPO  Host fail RTO/RPO  Site loss RTO/RPO         Restore  Verdict
------------  --------------  -----------------  ------------------------  -------  -------
web-frontend  72h / 0h        6.25h / 15m        ∞ (cannot recover) / 15m  2.25h    GAPS
edge-fw       72h / 1h        0h / 0h            not required              9m       GAPS
erp-legacy    1h / 15m        15m / 24h          not required              2.25h    GAPS

--- Step 2 — Gaps and cheapest fixes ----------------------------------------
web-frontend — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 15m of data lost > target 0h
  • SITE: no recovery site, so nowhere to restore to after a site loss
  • SITE RPO: after a site loss up to 15m of data is lost > target 0h
  • POWER: UPS + generator run 10.2m < required 8h
  • TEST: backup restore last tested 2025-06-21 (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add synchronous replication (RPO 0h, $120,000/yr)
  • → Use a warm site (ready in 24h, $150,000/yr)
  • → Add a generator (a UPS only bridges minutes)
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO
edge-fw — GAPS
  • TEST: DR failover never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Schedule a failover test / simulation / parallel processing and record the measured RTO/RPO
erp-legacy — GAPS
  • RPO: up to 24h of data lost > target 15m
  • DISK: RAID5 tolerates 1 disk failure(s) < required 2
  • TEST: backup restore never tested (untested plan = no plan)
  • → Add asynchronous replication (RPO 15m, $40,000/yr)
  • → Rebuild storage as RAID6 (tolerates 2, 67% usable capacity)
  • → Schedule a restore test and record the measured RTO/RPO

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.4 Resilience & recovery: sites, replication, backups,
| high availability, power, testing.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • RPO is answered by backup frequency or replication; RTO by failover
| (clustering) or how fast a site can take over.
|   • Hot = running and synced (expensive); warm = hardware ready, restore
| data; cold = space and power only.
|   • Incremental backups are fastest to take but slowest to restore;
| differential is in between; full restores fastest.
|   • RAID is availability, not backup: RAID1/5/10 survive one disk, RAID6
| survives two, RAID0 survives none.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Nightly backups for a system the business assumed loses at most 4
| hours of data.
|   • Backups stored in the same building that floods.
|   • A UPS with no generator, so it buys 10 minutes for a 4-hour outage.
|   • A DR plan never tested; the first failover is during the real
| disaster.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • An AI operations agent can trigger failover automatically only for
| pre-approved, tested runbooks.
|   • Agents must not delete or shorten backup retention; backups are a
| protected control (Lab 5).
|   • Use agents to run and record restore tests continuously, turning
| 'untested' into measured RTO/RPO.
|   • Declaring a disaster (moving to the alternate site) stays a human
| decision.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • Load balancing spreads load across active nodes; clustering adds
| failover. Both are high availability.
|   • Geographic dispersion protects against regional disasters; multi-cloud
| protects against provider failure.
|   • Testing types: tabletop (discussion), simulation, fail over, parallel
| processing (run both systems).
|   • UPS = short-term power + clean shutdown; generator = long-term power.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

VN-4 Riverbend Co-Marketing → APPROVE_WITH_CONDITIONS · monitoring: annual reassessment
  • CONDITION: add the missing 'BPA' clause/agreement (an MOU is a non-binding statement of intent and does not replace it)
  • 3 questionnaire gap(s), e.g. Q05 Incident response plan tested in the last 12 months: partial
VN-5 NetOps MSP → REJECT · monitoring: quarterly reviews + continuous monitoring
  • REJECT: conflict of interest not disclosed/cleared: due diligence failed
  • CONDITION: residual risk 13.32 is MEDIUM: agree a remediation plan for the questionnaire gaps

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 5.3 Third-party risk: assessment, due diligence,
| agreement types, monitoring.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Inherent vendor risk comes from what the vendor touches: data
| sensitivity, network/privileged access, criticality.
|   • Questionnaires, independent assessments (SOC 2, ISO 27001), pen tests
| and right-to-audit are how you VERIFY a vendor.
|   • Agreements: MSA (umbrella terms), SOW/WO (specific work), SLA
| (measurable service), NDA, BPA (partnership), MOU/MOA (intent/agreement).
|   • Vendor risk is continuous: monitor on a cadence matching the risk, and
| analyse their suppliers too (fourth parties).
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Giving an HVAC contractor network access with no security requirements
| (how the 2013 Target breach began).
|   • Signing a non-binding MOU where a binding agreement (BPA/MSA) was
| needed.
|   • No right-to-audit and no independent assessment: you are trusting a
| marketing slide.
|   • Skipping conflict-of-interest checks during selection.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • AI vendors are third parties too: assess model providers for data use,
| retention, subprocessors and audit rights.
|   • An AI procurement assistant can pre-score questionnaires, but approval
| and contract sign-off are human decisions.
|   • Vendor answers are untrusted input: an agent reading questionnaires
| must not follow instructions embedded in them.
|   • Keep agent-derived scores reproducible: same answers + same policy =
| same score, with every gap listed.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Allows the customer to inspect the vendor's security controls' =
| right-to-audit clause.
|   • 'Defines expected uptime and response times' = SLA. 'Umbrella contract
| for future work' = MSA.
|   • MOU = intent, typically not legally binding. BPA = partner
| responsibilities and profit sharing.
|   • Supply chain analysis looks at the vendor's own vendors and components
| (e.g. SBOM).
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 2 — Why, and how to fix it -----------------------------------------
P-01 Healthy e-commerce site → TRUSTED
  • Valid chain, name, strength, usage and revocation status.
P-02 API certificate nobody renewed → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR EXPIRED: 'api.delzarsolutions.com' expired on 2026-10-31
  • Fix: Renew and automate renewal (ACME); monitor expiry dates.
P-03 Wildcard stretched one level too far → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR HOSTNAME_MISMATCH: 'dev.portal.delzarsolutions.com' is not covered by ['*.delzarsolutions.com', 'delzarsolutions.com']
  • Fix: Re-issue with the correct SAN entries (a wildcard covers only one label).
P-04 Server forgot to send its intermediate → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR INCOMPLETE_CHAIN: issuer 'GlobalTrust TLS CA 3' was not sent and is not a trusted root (missing intermediate)
  • Fix: Configure the server to send the full chain (leaf + intermediates).
P-05 Self-signed admin console → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR SELF_SIGNED: 'admin.internal' is self-signed and not in the trust store
  • WARNING VALIDITY_TOO_LONG: leaf is valid for 3652 days (> 398)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Issue the certificate from your internal CA (or a public CA); don't train users to click through warnings.
P-06 Certificate revoked after key compromise → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR REVOKED: 'vpn.delzarsolutions.com' (serial 1006) is revoked (CRL from Delzar Issuing CA 1)
  • Fix: Replace the certificate now; it was revoked (often key compromise). Investigate the key.
P-07 Legacy appliance with old crypto → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR WEAK_KEY: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' uses RSA-1024 (< 2048)
  • ERROR WEAK_SIGNATURE: 'printer.delzarsolutions.com' is signed with sha1WithRSAEncryption
  • Fix: Generate a new key pair (RSA ≥ 2048 or EC P-256+) and a new CSR.
P-08 Mobile banking app behind a TLS-inspection proxy → UNTRUSTED
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 28 days (2026-12-01)
  • ERROR PIN_MISMATCH: presented key 0dd1e57ab1e5… is not one of the app's pinned keys
  • Fix: Treat as interception: verify the network path / proxy; never disable the pin to 'make it work'.
P-09 Renewal due, revocation server unreachable → TRUSTED_WITH_WARNINGS
  • WARNING EXPIRING_SOON: leaf expires in 17 days (2026-11-20)
  • WARNING REVOCATION_UNKNOWN: no OCSP answer and no CRL for the leaf; status cannot be confirmed
  • Fix: Enable OCSP stapling so clients always get a fresh revocation status.
P-10 A leaf certificate used to sign another → UNTRUSTED
  • ERROR NOT_A_CA: 'shop.delzarsolutions.com' signed 'store.delzarsolutions.com' but is not a CA (basicConstraints CA:FALSE)
  • Fix: Re-issue from a real CA: a leaf certificate (CA:FALSE) cannot sign other certificates.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 1.4 Public key infrastructure, certificates and
| revocation.
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Trust flows down a chain: root (trust anchor, self-signed) →
| intermediate CA → leaf. Every link must be valid and every issuer a CA.
|   • Revocation: CRLs are lists you download; OCSP asks about one
| certificate in real time; OCSP stapling lets the server deliver it.
|   • Names come from the SAN; a wildcard covers exactly one label
| (*.example.com ≠ a.b.example.com, ≠ example.com).
|   • Key length and algorithm matter: RSA ≥ 2048 / EC ≥ 256 bits with SHA-2
| signatures; SHA-1 and MD5 are broken.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Servers that send only the leaf certificate: works in some browsers
| (cached intermediates), fails in apps and APIs.
|   • Training users to click through self-signed certificate warnings,
| which makes MITM attacks invisible.
|   • Soft-fail revocation checking: an attacker who blocks OCSP makes a
| revoked certificate look fine.
|   • Expired certificates taking down production because renewal was a
| calendar reminder, not automation.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Agents that call APIs must validate certificates and must never be
| configured with 'verify=False'.
|   • An AI ops agent may renew certificates through ACME, but issuing from
| the internal CA or adding trust anchors needs a human.
|   • Pin the endpoints your agents depend on; a PIN_MISMATCH should stop
| the agent, not be retried around.
|   • Private keys (including agents' own signing keys) belong in an
| HSM/KMS, never in prompts, logs or tickets.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Real-time status of a single certificate' = OCSP; 'downloaded list of
| revoked serials' = CRL.
|   • 'Covers all first-level subdomains' = wildcard certificate; 'lists
| several different names' = SAN.
|   • 'Request sent to a CA containing the public key' = CSR. 'Third party
| holds a copy of keys' = key escrow.
|   • Root of trust = the CA certificate in the trust store that everything
| else chains to.

| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.

| PII must not reach an external model.

| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.

| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.

| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

  • regulated data at_rest has protection (none); needs encryption or tokenization or masking or hashing: encrypt at rest (e.g. AES-256)

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Content inspection
Flow  Declared    Detections                                Effective

--- Step 2 — DLP decision per outbound flow ---------------------------------

Flows
Flow  State       Destination      Protection                            Decision
----  ----------  ---------------  ------------------------------------  --------
DF-1  in_transit  internal_app@us  tokenization + TLS channel            ALLOW
DF-2  in_use      analytics@us     masking + permission_restrictions     BLOCK
DF-3  in_transit  internal_app@us  masking + tokenization + TLS channel  ALLOW
DF-4  in_use      internal_app@us  tokenization + encryption             ALLOW
DF-5  at_rest     internal_app@eu  none                                  BLOCK
  DF-1 generated flow (health)                   ALLOW  restricted
  • content found (medical record number (PHI)) raises the label from public to restricted
  • restricted data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-2 generated flow (password)                 BLOCK  critical
  • content found (password) raises the label from public to critical
  • critical data may not go to a 'analytics' destination
  DF-3 generated flow (legal)                    ALLOW  confidential
  • content found (privileged legal material) raises the label from private to confidential
  • confidential data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-4 generated flow (email)                    ALLOW  restricted
  • restricted data to an approved internal_app in us; protection meets policy
  DF-5 generated flow (password)                 BLOCK  critical
  • content found (password) raises the label from private to critical
  • critical data may not go to a 'internal_app' destination
  • critical data may only be in us, not region 'eu'
  • credential data at_rest has protection (none); needs hashing: store only a salted, key-stretched hash (bcrypt/PBKDF2/Argon2), never reversible encryption

--- Step 3 — Protection methods ---------------------------------------------
  • Encryption: reversibly transforms data with a key so only key holders can read it (at rest: AES; in transit: TLS/IPsec).
  • Hashing: one-way fixed-length digest that cannot be reversed; salt + key stretching for stored passwords.
  • Masking: hides part of a value on display or in copies (e.g. ************1111) while keeping its format.
  • Tokenization: replaces the value with a random surrogate token; the real value is mapped in a secure token vault.
  • Obfuscation: makes data or code hard to understand without a key (e.g. code obfuscation, steganography).
  • Segmentation: keeps sensitive data in separate networks/systems so a breach of one does not expose all.
  • Permission restrictions: access controls (least privilege, ACLs) limit who can read or change the data.
  • Geographic restrictions: allow storage or access only from approved locations (geolocation / geofencing).

+-- Exam & Architectural Insight ------------------------------------------
| Objective: SY0-701 3.3 Data protection: types, classifications, states,
| sovereignty, methods (with 4.5 DLP).
| 
| Key Concepts
|   • Data types: regulated (PII, PHI, PCI), trade secret, intellectual
| property, legal, financial; human- or non-human-readable.
|   • Classify by the most sensitive content found, not by the label someone
| typed; the label drives handling rules.
|   • States: at rest (disk/database: encrypt, tokenize), in transit
| (TLS/IPsec), in use (memory/screen: mask, restrict).
|   • Data sovereignty: data is subject to the laws of the country where it
| is collected/stored; geolocation enforces it.
|   • Masking hides digits, tokenization swaps in a vault-mapped surrogate,
| hashing is one-way, encryption is reversible.
| 
| Manual Failure Modes
|   • Storing passwords with reversible encryption: steal the key and you
| have every password (hash + salt instead).
|   • A regex that flags every 16-digit number: alert fatigue until DLP is
| ignored (validate PANs with Luhn).
|   • Exporting EU customer data to a cheaper overseas region and breaking
| data sovereignty rules.
|   • Showing full card numbers to support staff who only need the last 4
| digits.
| 
| How to Govern an AI Agent Here
|   • Put a DLP gate in front of prompts and agent tool calls: secrets and
| PII must not reach an external model.
|   • AI agents need data-handling rules by classification, the same as
| people: least privilege on data, not just systems.
|   • Region-pin AI model endpoints and logs for regulated data; prompts are
| data in transit and at rest too.
|   • Content returned to an agent is untrusted: an 'ignore the DLP policy'
| line in a record is data, not an instruction.
| 
| Exam Tips
|   • 'Replaces the value with a random surrogate mapped in a vault' =
| tokenization. 'Shows only the last 4' = masking.
|   • Passwords: salted hashing (plus key stretching such as bcrypt/PBKDF2),
| never encryption.
|   • Data in transit → TLS/IPsec/VPN. Data at rest → full-
| disk/database/file encryption. Data in use → hardest to protect.
|   • Data sovereignty = the law of the country where the data resides;
| geographic restrictions/geofencing enforce it.
|   • DLP can sit on endpoints, the network or in the cloud, and can alert,
| block or quarantine transfers.
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

52 events from sources: app, auth, dns, edr, firewall

Alerts
ID     Rule                                    Severity  Time       Entities                                  Evidence                 Disposition

AL-01  SIEM-006 Threat-intel match             high      02:00:00Z  indicator=update-checker.example.net, so  EV-05                    ALERT
AL-02  SIEM-006 Threat-intel match             high      02:05:00Z  indicator=192.0.2.66, source_host=10.0.3  EV-06                    ALERT
AL-03  SIEM-004 After-hours privileged action  high      02:14:00Z  user=mlee, host=ERP-1                     EV-07                    ALERT
AL-04  SIEM-001 Brute force                    critical  03:01:00Z  user=jdoe, src_ip=203.0.113.50            EV-09, EV-10, EV-11 ...  ALERT
